<math><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>(</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>)</mo><mspace width="0.25em"/><mtext>mod</mtext><mspace width="0.25em"/><mn>26</mn><mo>:</mo><mspace width="0.5em"/><mtext>A</mtext><mo>→</mo><mo>(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>)</mo><mspace width="0.25em"/><mtext>mod</mtext><mspace width="0.25em"/><mn>26</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>19</mn><mo>→</mo><mtext>T</mtext></math>

Running the subtraction across the whole ciphertext: T (19) - 7 = 12 = M; L (11) - 7 = 4 = E, twice; A (0) - 7 = -7, and -7 mod 26 = 19 = T, the wrap-around going backwards; H (7) - 7 = 0 = A; A again gives T; U (20) - 7 = 13 = N; V (21) - 7 = 14 = O, twice; U gives N. TLLA HA UVVU decrypts back to MEET AT NOON. Two things are worth noticing. First, encryption and decryption are inverse operations on the same key, which makes the Caesar cipher symmetric — sender and receiver must both know that k = 7. Second, negative results still need the modulo: in many programming languages the built-in % operator returns a negative value for -7 % 26, so implementations usually add 26 before taking the modulus.

entries.label: Treating sampling rate and bit depth as the same knob

content.value: These are independent, and they degrade the signal in different ways. Sampling rate (or, for images, resolution) is how many measurements you take along time or space; bit depth (or color depth) is how precisely each single measurement is stored. Doubling the sampling rate does nothing to fix banding in a gradient, and doubling the bit depth does nothing to recover detail that was never sampled. A quick check: if the problem is blockiness, blur, or missing fine detail, that points to sampling; if the problem is a stepped, posterized, or hissy quality where the values should change smoothly, that points to bit depth. Also keep both distinct from compression, which is a separate step applied after digitization and may be lossless or lossy.

entries.label: Assuming a substitution cipher is actually secure

content.value: The Caesar cipher is a teaching device, not a security mechanism. It has only 25 useful keys, so brute force means trying at most 25 shifts — trivial by hand and instantaneous by computer. Even a general substitution cipher with an arbitrary scrambled alphabet, which has a far larger keyspace, falls quickly to frequency analysis: because each plaintext letter always maps to the same ciphertext letter, the statistical fingerprint of the language survives encryption. In English, E is the most common letter, so the most common ciphertext symbol in a long enough message is very likely E; repeated patterns and one-letter words fill in the rest. A large keyspace is necessary for security but nowhere near sufficient — the cipher must also destroy the patterns in the plaintext, which is exactly what modern block ciphers are engineered to do.

entries.label: Mixing up which asymmetric key does what

content.value: The most frequent error is thinking you encrypt with your own public key, or that the private key is what you hand out. To send someone a confidential message you encrypt with the recipient's public key, and only their private key can open it — your own keys play no part in that direction. Signing runs the opposite way: you sign with your private key so that anyone with your public key can verify it came from you. Confidentiality uses the recipient's key pair; authenticity uses the sender's. A related mistake is claiming asymmetric encryption has simply replaced symmetric encryption. It has not — it is far slower, so secure systems use it briefly to establish a shared symmetric key and then encrypt the actual data symmetrically.

sections.heading: Models, Simulation, and Working with Data

content.value:
A model is a simplified representation of a real system, built to answer a specific question about that system. The word simplified is the important part: a model deliberately leaves things out. A model of a town's population might track only the current head count and a yearly growth rate, ignoring individual people entirely, because the question being asked is "roughly how many residents in ten years?" A model of a traffic light might track only the current colour and how many seconds it has been that colour, ignoring the cars, the weather, and the road surface.

Building a model means choosing the variables that matter to the question and discarding everything else. Those choices are the model's assumptions. A model is never right or wrong in an absolute sense; it is useful or not useful for a particular question, and that usefulness depends entirely on whether the discarded details actually mattered.

Simulation is running a model to see what happens. Where a model is the description of the system, a simulation is the execution of that description, usually stepped forward through time or through a set of scenarios.

A typical simulation has a state (the current values of the model's variables), a set of update rules (how the state changes from one step to the next), and a stopping condition (a number of steps, or a target value being reached). The program applies the rules over and over and records the state along the way.

Simulation is used when the real experiment is too slow, too expensive, too dangerous, or simply impossible: you cannot rerun a hurricane, wait fifty years for a forest, or crash a hundred real cars. It is also used when a system has no clean closed-form answer, so the only practical way to see the outcome is to step through it.

Every model sits somewhere on a scale between too simple and too complex, and both ends have real costs.

Too little detail: the model omits a variable that actually drives the behaviour, so its output is confidently wrong. A population model with a fixed growth rate will not predict a crash caused by running out of food, because food was never in the model.

Too much detail: the model becomes expensive to run, slower to develop, harder to explain, and harder to debug. It also needs more input data, and each extra input is another number that might be measured badly. A model with fifty parameters can be tuned to match past data perfectly and still fail on new data.

The practical rule is to include the variables the question depends on and no more, then test whether adding one more detail actually changes the conclusion. If it does not, leave it out.

Simulations produce data, and so does the real world. Three operations cover most of what is done with a table of records, whether in a spreadsheet, a database query, or a loop in code.

Filtering (selecting) keeps only the rows that satisfy a condition and drops the rest. "Only the students who scored 70 or above." Filtering changes how many rows you have but not what each row contains.

Aggregating (summarizing) collapses many rows into a single value: a sum, a count, an average, a minimum, a maximum. Aggregation destroys the individual rows; once you have the average you cannot recover the values that produced it.

Sorting reorders the rows by the value in some column, ascending or descending. Sorting changes neither the number of rows nor their contents, which is why it is safe to do at any point; it is used to find the top few items or to make a result readable.

A fourth operation, grouping, combines the first two: split the rows into groups by the value of some column, then aggregate within each group, producing one summary row per group.

A deterministic model produces exactly the same output every time it is run with the same inputs. A population that grows by exactly 8 percent per year is deterministic: run it a thousand times and you get one answer.

A stochastic (random) model includes randomness, so each run gives a different result. A model where each customer arrives at a random time, or each coin flip is random, is stochastic. A single run of a stochastic model tells you very little, because it is one sample. That is why such models are run many times and the results aggregated: run the simulation 10,000 times, then report the average outcome and how widely the outcomes spread.

This is the practical reason simulations are described as being run "repeatedly": with a deterministic model repetition is pointless, but with a stochastic one a single run can easily be an unrepresentative outlier.

Question: a town has 2,000 residents and has been growing at about 8 percent per year. If that rate holds, what is the population after 4 years?

The model: one state variable, population, and one rule, population at the end of a year equals population at the start of the year multiplied by 1.08. One step of the simulation equals one year.

What this model assumes: the growth rate stays exactly 8 percent every year; growth compounds once at year end; nothing limits growth such as housing, jobs, or land; and population can be a fractional number between reporting points. Every one of those assumptions is false in some detail about the real town. They are stated up front so the output can be read honestly.

Trace the loop by hand, keeping the running value rather than rounding at each step.

Start: population = 2000, year = 0.

Year 1: 2000 x 1.08 = 2160. Now population = 2160, year = 1. Growth this year: 160 residents.

Year 2: 2160 x 1.08 = 2332.8. Now population = 2332.8, year = 2. Growth this year: 172.8 residents.

Notice that the second year adds more people than the first even though the rate did not change. That is compounding: the 8 percent is applied to a larger base each time. Reading a trace table is the standard way to check that a simulation's update rule is doing what you intended.

Year 3: 2332.8 x 1.08 = 2519.424. Now population = 2519.424, year = 3. Growth this year: 186.624 residents.

Year 4: 2519.424 x 1.08 = 2720.97792. Now population = 2720.97792, year = 4. Growth this year: 201.55392 residents.

The loop condition year < 4 is now false, so the simulation stops. The answer to the original question is about 2,721 residents, and the rounding to a whole number happens once at the end, when reporting, not at every step.

The simulation produced a small dataset: the year-end populations 2160, 2332.8, 2519.424, and 2720.97792. Aggregating it answers follow-up questions.

Sum of the four year-end values: 2160 + 2332.8 = 4492.8; 4492.8 + 2519.424 = 7012.224; 7012.224 + 2720.97792 = 9733.20192.

Average year-end population: 9733.20192 / 4 = 2433.30048, so about 2,433.

Total growth over the run: 2720.97792 - 2000 = 720.97792, about 721 residents, which is roughly 36.05 percent of the starting population.

That last figure is worth pausing on. Multiplying 8 percent by 4 years gives 32 percent, but the simulation gives about 36 percent. The extra 4 percentage points are compounding, and they are exactly the kind of behaviour that stepping a model through time captures and a back-of-the-envelope multiplication misses.

The correct statement of the result is: under this model's assumptions, the population after 4 years is about 2,721. It is not "the town will have 2,721 residents."

The output inherits every assumption in the model. If the real growth rate averages 6 percent rather than 8, the year-4 result is 2000 x 1.06^4 = about 2525, roughly 200 fewer people; a 2-point error in one input moved the answer by about 7 percent. If the town runs out of buildable land in year 3, the model has no way to represent that at all and will keep growing forever.

Testing how much the output moves when an input is changed is called sensitivity analysis, and it is a normal part of using a model. Rerunning at 6 percent and at 10 percent gives a range rather than a single misleadingly precise number.

entries.label: Treating model output as a guaranteed prediction

content.value:
The most common error is reading a simulation's output as a statement about the future rather than as a conditional result. A model says "if these rules and these inputs hold, this follows." It does not say "this will happen."

The error is made worse by precision. A result of 2720.97792 looks far more authoritative than "roughly 2,700," but the extra digits come from the arithmetic, not from any extra knowledge about the town. Precision in the output can never exceed the accuracy of the inputs and the fidelity of the rules.

The fix is to report the assumptions alongside the number, and to report a range from several plausible inputs rather than one figure carried to five decimal places.

A model is built to answer one question over one range of conditions, and it is easy to keep using it outside that range because it keeps returning numbers. Software does not refuse; a fixed-rate growth model asked for year 200 will happily report tens of millions of residents in a town with room for ten thousand.

Related versions of the same mistake: reusing a model built for one system on a different system because the shapes look alike; continuing to use a model after the world changed, so an assumption that held when it was written is now false; and forgetting that a discarded variable was discarded, then treating the model's silence about it as evidence that it does not matter.

The fix is to write the model's assumptions and its valid range down next to the model, and to check the question against that list before trusting an answer.

When filtering and aggregating are combined, the order changes the answer, and aggregating first is usually the mistake, because aggregation destroys the rows the filter was supposed to examine.

Take five test scores: 55, 72, 90, 68, 80. Question: what is the average score among students who passed, where passing is 70 or above?

Wrong order (aggregate, then filter): the average of all five is (55 + 72 + 90 + 68 + 80) / 5 = 365 / 5 = 73. That single value 73 is above 70, so it survives any later filter, and 73 gets reported. But 73 is the average of everyone, passing and failing, and answers a different question.

Right order (filter, then aggregate): keep 72, 90, and 80. Their sum is 242, and 242 / 3 = 80.67. The correct answer is about 80.67, nearly 8 points higher.

The general rule is that filters restricting which records count must be applied before the aggregate is computed. A condition on the aggregate itself, such as "show only groups whose average is above 75," is genuinely applied afterward. Confusing these two kinds of condition is exactly the distinction that WHERE and HAVING draw in SQL.

sections.heading: What an operating system does, and the machine underneath it

content.value: Bare hardware does exactly one thing: it executes machine instructions. It has no notion of a "file", a "window", or "two programs at once". The operating system is the layer of software that sits between applications and hardware and supplies those notions. It exists for two reasons. First, abstraction: without it, every application author would have to write code specific to each brand of disk, each network card, each keyboard. The OS hides that variety behind uniform interfaces, so a program calls "open this file" or "send these bytes" and the OS translates the request into whatever the actual device requires. Second, arbitration: the CPU, the memory, and the disk are finite shared resources, and multiple programs want them simultaneously. Someone has to decide who gets what, and when, and has to stop one program from reading or corrupting another's data. That referee is the OS.

entries.label: The four things an OS manages

content.value: OS responsibilities are conventionally grouped into four areas. (1) Process management: creating, scheduling, suspending, and terminating running programs, and giving each one the illusion that it has the CPU to itself. (2) Memory management: assigning each process a region of RAM, keeping processes out of each other's memory, and reclaiming memory when a process ends. Modern systems use virtual memory, in which each process sees its own private address space that the OS (with hardware help) maps onto real physical memory — and can temporarily move data out to disk when RAM runs short. (3) File system management: organizing persistent storage into named files and directories, tracking where each file's blocks physically live, and enforcing permissions on who may read or write them. (4) Device and I/O management: talking to keyboards, displays, disks, and network interfaces through device drivers, and buffering data between fast components and slow ones.

entries.label: Scheduling and the illusion of simultaneity

content.value: A single CPU core can execute only one instruction stream at a time, yet a laptop appears to run a browser, a music player, and a text editor at once. The OS achieves this by time-slicing: the scheduler gives one process the CPU for a few milliseconds, then performs a context switch — saving that process's registers and program counter, loading another process's saved state, and resuming it. Switching happens fast enough that a human perceives continuous, simultaneous execution. This is concurrency (tasks interleaved and making progress over the same period), which is distinct from true parallelism (tasks literally executing at the same instant on separate cores). A scheduler must balance competing goals: keeping the CPU busy, giving interactive tasks fast response, and preventing any process from being starved of CPU time indefinitely.

entries.label: Basic architecture: CPU, RAM, storage, I/O

content.value: Four components and the buses connecting them account for most of what a computer does. The CPU executes instructions and contains a small number of extremely fast registers plus a control unit and an arithmetic/logic unit (ALU) that performs arithmetic and comparisons. RAM (main memory) holds the instructions and data of currently running programs; it is fast, directly addressable by the CPU, and volatile — its contents vanish when power is lost. Secondary storage (SSD or hard disk) is persistent and much larger, but far slower, and the CPU cannot execute instructions directly from it: data must be loaded into RAM first. I/O devices — keyboard, display, network interface — move data between the machine and the outside world. A useful mental model is a hierarchy ordered by speed and cost: registers, then CPU cache, then RAM, then storage. Registers, cache, and RAM each step down by roughly an order of magnitude in speed and up in size; the final step to storage is far bigger than that — RAM answers in tens of nanoseconds, while even a fast SSD takes tens of microseconds, roughly a thousand-fold jump, and a traditional spinning hard disk is slower still. A great deal of system design amounts to keeping the data you need soon as high up that hierarchy as possible, precisely because that last gap is so large.

At the lowest level the CPU repeats one loop, billions of times per second. Fetch: the CPU reads the instruction stored at the address held in the program counter. Decode: the control unit interprets the instruction's bit pattern to determine the operation and its operands. Execute: the operation is carried out — an ALU calculation, a load from or store to memory, or a jump. Then the program counter advances to the next instruction (or is set to a new address if the instruction was a branch) and the cycle repeats. Everything a computer does — rendering video, running a compiler, serving a web page — is this cycle repeated over an enormous number of very simple steps. It is also why a stored-program computer is general purpose: instructions live in the same memory as data, so loading different bytes into memory turns the machine into a different application.

When two devices communicate, the most common arrangement is client-server. The client initiates: it sends a request for a resource or an action. The server waits, listens for incoming requests, performs the work, and sends back a response. The roles are defined by behavior in a particular exchange, not by hardware — the same machine can be a server for one conversation and a client in another. Servers are typically always available at a known address, and a single server usually handles many clients. Communication follows a protocol, an agreed set of rules about message format and ordering, so that machines built by different manufacturers and running different operating systems can interoperate; HTTP is the protocol for web requests. The contrasting arrangement is peer-to-peer, where every participant can both request and supply, with no central authority. Client-server is simpler to secure and administer but creates a single point of failure; peer-to-peer degrades more gracefully but is harder to control.

sections.heading: Worked example: what happens when a user opens a browser and loads a page

content.value: A student double-clicks a browser icon, types a web address, and presses Enter. A few hundred milliseconds later a page appears. Trace what the operating system, the hardware, and the network each contribute — from the click to the rendered page. This single scenario touches nearly every idea in this category, which is why it is worth walking end to end rather than memorizing the pieces separately.

entries.label: Step 1 — the OS creates a process

content.value: The double-click is an I/O event: the mouse driver reports it, and the OS delivers it to the desktop environment, which asks the OS to launch the browser. The OS locates the browser's executable file on storage through the file system, checks that the user has permission to execute it, and creates a new process. Creating a process means building a bookkeeping record — a process control block — that holds a unique process ID, the process's current state, its saved register values, and its memory boundaries. The executable's instructions are read from slow persistent storage into RAM, because the CPU can only execute from memory. The program (the file sitting on disk) has now become a process (a running instance with its own memory and its own place in the scheduler's queue).

entries.label: Step 2 — memory is allocated and the CPU begins executing

content.value: The OS gives the new process an address space: a region for its instructions, a region for static data, a stack for function calls and local variables, and a heap for memory the program requests as it runs. Those addresses are virtual — the OS and the memory-management hardware translate them to physical RAM locations, which is what keeps this process from reading the memory of any other. The scheduler then places the process in the ready queue; when its turn comes, the CPU's program counter is set to the program's entry point and the fetch-decode-execute cycle begins running browser code. The browser draws its window by asking the OS to write to the display, since it has no direct access to the graphics hardware itself.

entries.label: Step 3 — the request travels to a server

content.value: The typed address arrives as another sequence of I/O events. Before the browser can open a connection it needs an IP address, and that resolution is normally done by the browser itself (checking its own cache first) or by a resolver library the browser calls, not by the OS kernel — the OS's role is to carry the resolver's own DNS query out over the network like any other request. Once an address is in hand, the browser makes a system call — a controlled request into the OS kernel — asking to open a network connection to that address; the OS carries out the low-level work of exchanging packets to establish it. HTTP is then sent over that connection: the browser is the client, and it is asking for a specific resource. The message is broken into packets and forwarded hop by hop across intermediate routers until it reaches the destination machine. Note what the specific thread waiting on this exchange is doing meanwhile: nothing — it is blocked, waiting on I/O — but the browser process as a whole is not frozen, since other threads keep servicing the rest of the interface. The scheduler hands the CPU to other processes (and other threads within this one) rather than letting it idle, which is part of why the rest of the machine stays responsive during a slow page load.

entries.label: Step 4 — the server responds and the browser renders

content.value: On the far end, a server program is running as a process under its own operating system, listening for incoming requests. It receives this one, reads the requested page from its file system or generates it from a database, and sends back a response containing a status code and the page's content. The packets travel back, the client OS reassembles them in order, and signals the waiting browser process that its data is ready. The scheduler moves the browser back to ready, then to running. The browser parses the returned HTML, requests any additional resources it references (images, stylesheets — each one another request-response exchange), computes a layout, and asks the OS to paint the result on screen. If the user saves the page, the reverse of step 1 occurs: bytes move from RAM back to persistent storage through the file system.

The whole sequence is one continuous chain of the category's core ideas: the OS turned a program into a process, allocated it memory, and mediated every access to hardware; the CPU did nothing but fetch, decode, and execute; data moved from storage into RAM to be worked on and back to storage to persist; and the two machines cooperated as client and server under a shared protocol. The most transferable lesson is the layering — the browser never touched the disk or the network card directly. It asked the OS, and the OS, which alone runs with the privilege to command hardware, did it on the browser's behalf. That is what makes it possible to run untrusted programs on a shared machine without them wrecking each other.

The most persistent beginner error is treating "memory" and "storage" as one thing — encouraged by everyday phrasing like "my phone is out of memory" when the disk is full. They differ on three axes. Volatility: RAM loses its contents the instant power is cut, which is why unsaved work disappears in a crash; storage persists. Speed: RAM is orders of magnitude faster, and the CPU can address it directly, whereas storage must be read in blocks into RAM before its contents can be used. Purpose: RAM holds what is being worked on right now; storage holds what must survive until later. The practical test for students is the save operation. If saving a file were merely a formality, RAM and storage would be the same thing. Saving exists precisely because it copies data from the volatile place to the persistent one. A related confusion is thinking a program "runs from the hard drive" — it is loaded from storage into RAM, and executes there.

entries.label: Assuming a server is always a big machine somewhere far away

content.value: "Server" names a role in a conversation, not a category of hardware and not a location. A server is any software that listens for requests and returns responses; the machine it happens to run on is incidental. Three consequences follow, and each shows up in exam items. First, a client and a server can be the same physical device: a student running a local web server for a class project sends requests from a browser to a server process on that same laptop, over the loopback address, with no network hop at all — which is why classroom web development works without internet access. Second, one machine can be both at once: a web server that queries a database is a server to the browser and a client to the database. Third, being a server has nothing to do with size — a thermostat, a printer, or a Raspberry Pi can serve requests. The complementary error is thinking "the cloud" is something other than ordinary servers in ordinary buildings, owned by someone else.

A program is passive: a file of instructions sitting in storage, doing nothing. A process is active: one running instance of that program, with its own memory, its own CPU state, and its own entry in the OS's process table. The distinction becomes concrete the moment you open the same application twice — one program, two processes, each with separate memory, so text typed in one window does not appear in the other. It also explains why "quitting" an application removes a process without deleting the program. A thread goes one level finer: a single flow of execution inside a process, sharing that process's memory with the other threads in it. That sharing is exactly why threads are efficient to switch between and also why they are hazardous — two threads writing the same variable can interleave badly, whereas two processes are isolated by default.

entries.label: Believing the OS is the desktop you can see

content.value: Students frequently equate the operating system with its graphical interface — the icons, windows, and menus. The interface is one program running on top of the OS, not the OS itself, which is why a server can run the same operating system with no graphical shell at all, and why changing the visual theme changes nothing about scheduling or memory management. The core of the OS is the kernel, invisible code that runs in a privileged mode of the CPU where it alone may command hardware directly. Ordinary programs run unprivileged and must cross into the kernel through system calls to do anything real — open a file, allocate memory, send a packet. That privilege boundary, not the appearance of the desktop, is what makes an operating system an operating system.

sections.heading: How networks and the Web work

entries.label: LAN, WAN, and the internet as a network of networks

content.value: A network is two or more computing devices connected so they can exchange data. A local area network (LAN) covers a small geographic area under a single administrative owner — a classroom, a building, a home. LANs are typically built from Ethernet cabling and Wi-Fi access points joined by switches, and because the distances are short they are fast and cheap to run. A wide area network (WAN) connects sites across cities, countries, or continents, usually over infrastructure leased from telecommunications carriers rather than owned outright; a district office linked to twelve school buildings is a WAN. The internet is the largest WAN, but the important idea for the exam is that it is not one network at all: it is a network of networks. Tens of thousands of independently owned and operated networks — university campuses, corporate LANs, residential ISPs, cloud data centers — agree to interconnect and to forward each other's traffic using a common set of protocols. No single organization owns it or controls its routing. Devices that join networks together are worth distinguishing: a switch forwards traffic within one LAN, while a router connects different networks to each other and decides which way to send traffic that is leaving the local network. Your home router is the boundary between your LAN and your ISP's network, which is itself a step toward the rest of the internet.

Every device that participates in an internet conversation needs an IP address — a numeric identifier that says where it is on the network. IPv4 addresses are 32 bits, written as four decimal numbers from 0 to 255 separated by dots (198.51.100.7). Because 32 bits allows only about 4.3 billion addresses and the world ran out, IPv6 was introduced with 128-bit addresses written as up to eight groups of hexadecimal digits; a run of all-zero groups can be compressed once, with "::", so 2001:0db8:85a3::8a2e:0370:7334 is short for eight groups even though only seven appear on the page. An IP address is not a permanent property of a machine; most devices are assigned one automatically by DHCP when they join a network, and a laptop gets a different address at school than it has at home. Humans, however, do not want to memorize numbers, so the Domain Name System (DNS) provides a distributed directory that maps human-readable domain names such as example.org onto IP addresses. DNS is hierarchical: the name is read right to left, from the root, through a top-level domain (.org, .edu, .gov), down to the domain and any subdomains (www.example.org). When a computer needs to resolve a name it asks a resolver, which queries the hierarchy on its behalf and caches the answer for a set period so the same lookup does not have to be repeated. The key conceptual point is that DNS is a translation service layered on top of the network — it does not carry your data, it only tells your computer what address to send the data to.

Data does not travel across the internet as one continuous stream. The sending computer breaks a message — an email, an image, a web page — into small chunks called packets. Each packet carries a header with the source IP address and the destination IP address, followed by its slice of the actual data; if the packet belongs to a TCP connection, the TCP header riding inside that data also carries a sequence number, which is what lets the receiving end detect loss and put packets back in order. This is packet switching, and it is the design choice that makes the internet resilient and efficient: many conversations can share the same links by interleaving their packets, and no pair of machines has to reserve a dedicated circuit. Routers move each packet one hop at a time. A router examines the destination address, consults its routing table, and forwards the packet toward whichever neighboring router seems to be a step closer; it does not know or need to know the whole path. Because each packet is routed independently, packets from the same message can travel different physical routes, arrive out of order, arrive damaged, or not arrive at all. Reassembly and repair are handled by the layer above: TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) numbers the packets, acknowledges what arrived, requests retransmission of what did not, and hands the receiving application an ordered, complete stream. UDP is the alternative that skips those guarantees for speed, which suits live video and games where a late packet is worthless anyway. The layered picture to remember is IP for addressing and delivery, TCP or UDP for transport behavior, and application protocols such as HTTP, SMTP, or DNS riding on top.

entries.label: The Web: HTTP, URLs, HTML, and CSS

content.value: The Web is an application built on top of the internet, not a synonym for it — email, file transfer, and streaming use the same internet without being part of the Web. The Web runs on a client-server, request-response model: a browser (the client) sends an HTTP request to a web server, and the server sends back an HTTP response. A URL specifies what to request and how. In https://www.example.org/courses/index.html?term=fall, the scheme is https, the host is www.example.org (the part DNS resolves), the path is /courses/index.html, and term=fall is a query string passed to the server. HTTP requests carry a method — GET to retrieve a resource, POST to submit data — plus headers. Responses carry a status code (200 for success, 301 for a permanent redirect, 404 for not found, 500 for a server-side error), headers describing the content, and usually a body. HTTP is stateless: each request is handled independently, and continuity such as a login session is reconstructed using cookies or tokens sent with every request. The body of a page response is typically HTML, a markup language whose tags describe structure and meaning — headings, paragraphs, lists, links, images. CSS is a separate language that describes presentation: color, spacing, typography, layout. Keeping structure in HTML and appearance in CSS is the separation-of-concerns principle applied to documents. JavaScript adds the third layer, behavior, running inside the browser to change the page after it has loaded.

entries.label: Security concepts: encryption, firewalls, and common threats

content.value: Because packets pass through equipment nobody in the conversation controls, anything sent in plaintext can in principle be read or altered in transit. HTTPS solves this by wrapping ordinary HTTP inside TLS (Transport Layer Security, the successor to SSL). TLS does three things: it authenticates the server using a digital certificate issued by a certificate authority, it negotiates a shared secret key using public-key cryptography, and it then encrypts the traffic with fast symmetric encryption so an eavesdropper sees only ciphertext and any tampering is detected. A firewall performs a different job — it filters traffic crossing a network boundary, allowing or blocking packets based on rules about ports, addresses, protocols, and sometimes application content. Firewalls decide what may pass; encryption decides who can read what passes. Threats worth recognizing include eavesdropping or packet sniffing on shared networks; man-in-the-middle attacks, where an attacker relays and possibly alters traffic between two parties who believe they are talking directly; denial-of-service and distributed denial-of-service attacks, which exhaust a server's capacity with floods of requests rather than stealing anything; spoofing, which forges a source address or identity; and phishing, a social attack that tricks a person into surrendering credentials and that no amount of encryption prevents. Defenses layer accordingly: encryption for confidentiality in transit, firewalls and access control at boundaries, authentication and strong credentials for identity, and user education for the human layer.

sections.heading: Worked example: typing a URL and pressing enter

entries.label: Steps 1-2: parse the URL, then resolve the name with DNS

content.value: Suppose a user types https://www.example.org/courses/index.html and presses enter. Step 1: the browser parses the URL into its parts — scheme https, host www.example.org, path /courses/index.html — and notes that https means port 443 and an encrypted connection by default. Step 2: the browser needs an IP address, because routers forward by address and know nothing about names. It checks caches in order, cheapest first: its own in-memory DNS cache, then the operating system cache and the local hosts file. On a miss it asks the configured DNS resolver, usually one run by the ISP or a public service. The resolver, if it too has no cached answer, walks the hierarchy: it asks a root server, which points it at the .org top-level domain servers; those point it at the authoritative name servers for example.org; and those return the address record for www.example.org — say 198.51.100.7. The answer travels back to the browser and is cached along the way for the record's time-to-live. Notice that this lookup is a complete network conversation of its own, finished before the first byte of the actual web request is sent. If DNS fails here, the browser reports that the site's address could not be found — a different failure from a site that resolves but does not respond.

entries.label: Steps 3-4: open a TCP connection, then negotiate TLS

content.value: Step 3: the browser opens a TCP connection to 198.51.100.7 on port 443. TCP begins with a three-way handshake — the client sends SYN, the server replies SYN-ACK, the client answers ACK — which confirms both directions work and establishes the sequence numbers used to order and acknowledge packets. Every packet in this exchange is routed hop by hop across the internet as described earlier; neither endpoint knows or controls the path. Step 4: because the scheme is https, TLS is negotiated on top of that TCP connection before any HTTP is sent. The client announces which cipher suites and TLS versions it supports; the server chooses one and presents its digital certificate. The browser validates that certificate — checking that it was issued by a certificate authority the browser trusts, that it has not expired or been revoked, and crucially that the name on the certificate matches www.example.org. If validation fails, the browser shows a security warning rather than proceeding. On success the two sides use public-key cryptography to agree on a symmetric session key, and from that point everything — the request line, headers, cookies, page content — is encrypted. This ordering is the point worth memorizing: DNS lookup, then TCP connection, then TLS handshake, then HTTP. TLS protects the HTTP conversation; it does not protect the DNS lookup that preceded it, which is why the domain being visited can still be observable on the network.

entries.label: Steps 5-6: the HTTP request and the server's response

content.value: Step 5: inside the encrypted channel the browser sends an HTTP request. The request line reads GET /courses/index.html HTTP/1.1, followed by headers — Host: www.example.org so a server hosting many sites on one address knows which is meant, User-Agent identifying the browser, Accept listing acceptable content types, and any Cookie values previously stored for this domain. A GET request has no body. Step 6: the web server receives the request, either returning a static file from disk or invoking application code that queries a database and generates the page. It replies with a status line — HTTP/1.1 200 OK for success, or 404 if the path does not exist, 301 or 302 to redirect the browser elsewhere, 500 if server-side code failed — plus response headers such as Content-Type: text/html and caching directives, and then the response body containing the HTML. Because HTTP is stateless, the server does not inherently remember this browser from one request to the next; if the user is logged in, that continuity comes from a session cookie or token included in each request. The entire response is broken into packets, transmitted, reassembled by TCP in the correct order, decrypted by TLS, and handed to the browser as a stream of HTML.

entries.label: Steps 7-8: rendering the page and fetching subresources

content.value: Step 7: the browser parses the HTML into a tree structure, the Document Object Model, which represents the nesting of elements. As it parses, it encounters references to other resources — a stylesheet at /css/site.css, images, fonts, script files, possibly assets on other domains entirely. Step 8: each of those is a separate HTTP request. Same-host resources reuse the existing connection where the protocol allows; resources on a different host trigger their own DNS lookup, connection, and TLS handshake. As CSS arrives the browser builds a style model, combines it with the DOM to compute the final appearance of each element, lays out the elements geometrically, and paints pixels to the screen. JavaScript that arrives may modify the DOM afterward, causing another layout and repaint, which is why a page can visibly change after it first appears. Because the HTML arrives first and subresources are fetched afterward, users often see unstyled or partially assembled content momentarily on a slow connection. When the user later clicks a link, the cycle repeats — though cached DNS answers, a warm TCP connection, a resumed TLS session, and cached CSS and images typically make subsequent pages load much faster than the first.

entries.label: Where a firewall inspects this sequence

content.value: A firewall sits at a network boundary and evaluates packets against rules at several points in the trace above. On the outbound side, a school or corporate firewall may check whether the destination port is permitted — 443 for HTTPS and 53 for DNS are normally allowed while unusual ports are blocked — and may compare the destination address or requested domain against a blocklist, refusing to let the connection open at all. It may force DNS queries through an approved internal resolver so that name resolution can be logged and filtered; a content filter that blocks a site typically acts at this DNS stage or on the connection attempt, which is why a blocked page often fails before any HTTP request is sent. On the inbound side, a firewall protecting the web server checks that arriving traffic is destined for a service that is supposed to be reachable — permitting 443 while dropping attempts to reach a database port — and a stateful firewall additionally tracks established connections so that response packets belonging to a conversation the inside started are allowed back in while unsolicited inbound packets are dropped. What the firewall generally cannot do is read the content of an HTTPS conversation once it is encrypted, since TLS protects the request and response bodies; but the TLS handshake itself is not fully hidden — the requested hostname is typically sent in the clear in the ClientHello's SNI field, so a firewall can and often does block or log connections by the domain name being requested, in addition to seeing addresses, ports, packet sizes, and timing. That is exactly how school and corporate content filters commonly enforce blocklists at the connection stage described above. Filtering on SNI has limits of its own — it can be evaded by protocols that encrypt the hostname — which is why organizations that want to see the actual page content, not just the domain, still need to filter at the DNS layer or deploy an inspection proxy that terminates and re-encrypts TLS.

entries.label: Confusing a domain name with an IP address

content.value: A domain name and an IP address are not the same identifier in two formats; they are entries on two sides of a lookup table maintained by an entirely separate system. The IP address is what the network actually uses to deliver packets, and routers have no knowledge of names at all. The domain name is a human convenience that must be translated by DNS before any data moves. The relationship is also not one-to-one in either direction: a single domain can map to many IP addresses for load balancing or geographic distribution, many domains can share one IP address on a shared host (which is why the HTTP Host header exists), and the address behind a name can change at any time. A related confusion is between a URL and a domain name — the domain is only the host portion of a URL, which also contains a scheme, a path, and possibly a query string and port. Two more distinctions commonly tested: an IP address identifies a device's position on a network and changes when it moves to a different network, whereas a MAC address is a hardware identifier burned into the network interface and used only within the local network segment. And a DNS failure produces a different symptom from a server failure — 'server not found' means the name could not be translated, while a 404 or a timeout means the name resolved fine and the problem lies further along.

entries.label: Assuming HTTPS means a site is trustworthy

content.value: The padlock and the https scheme make exactly two guarantees, and neither is about the site's honesty. First, the connection is encrypted, so someone watching the network cannot read or silently alter the traffic. Second, the certificate shows that the server genuinely controls the domain name shown in the address bar, so you are talking to whoever owns that name rather than an impostor intercepting the connection. What HTTPS does not tell you is whether that domain's owner is legitimate, whether the site sells real products, whether it will handle your data responsibly, or whether it is a phishing page. Basic domain-validated certificates are free and automated, so criminals obtain them routinely; a phishing site at a lookalike domain will show a perfectly valid padlock while encrypting your stolen password on its way to the attacker. The security question HTTPS answers is 'is this conversation private and is this really the domain named?' — not 'is this domain worth trusting?' Judging trustworthiness means reading the domain name character by character for lookalikes, considering how you arrived at the page, and being suspicious of unexpected requests for credentials. Conversely, a plain-http page is not necessarily malicious, but anything typed into it travels in readable form and should be treated as public.

These three defenses are often lumped together as 'security software,' but each addresses a distinct threat and none substitutes for the others. A traditional firewall controls traffic at a network boundary, deciding which packets may cross based on addresses, ports, protocols, and connection state; it is a gatekeeper rather than a content scanner. A basic packet-filtering firewall does not examine the contents of files and cannot tell whether a program is malicious — some more advanced firewalls do inspect limited application-level signals, such as a requested hostname, but reading and scanning full file contents is still fundamentally antivirus's job, not the firewall's. Antivirus or anti-malware software runs on a host and inspects files, processes, and behavior for known malicious signatures or suspicious activity; it can catch a virus in a downloaded attachment, which a firewall that permitted the download would never notice. Encryption makes data unreadable to anyone lacking the key, protecting confidentiality in transit (TLS) or at rest (disk encryption); it neither blocks nor detects anything, and it will faithfully protect malware in transit just as well as legitimate data. The practical consequences are worth stating plainly: a firewall will not stop a user from installing malware they deliberately downloaded over an allowed port, antivirus will not stop a denial-of-service flood aimed at a server, and encryption will not stop a phishing victim from typing a password into an attacker's form. Effective security uses all three in layers, together with authentication and access control, on the assumption that any single layer may fail.
